front.title: The agent URI Scheme and Verifiable Agent Identity

abstract.t: Software agents increasingly act on the Internet on behalf of people and organizations: they call APIs, browse websites, and delegate work to other agents. Protocols such as A2A and MCP define how agents communicate, but there is no interoperable way to answer a prior question: which agent is this, who operates it, and how can its claims be verified?

This document defines the agent URI scheme as a stable, human-readable identifier for an agent, a deterministic mapping from that identifier to an HTTPS-hosted Agent Identity Document, and a small set of mechanisms built on existing standards that let an agent prove its identity: signed statements binding the agent to its protocol metadata, an HTTP Message Signatures profile for requests made by the agent, short-lived credentials for ephemeral agent instances, and bindings to OAuth 2.0. It deliberately does not define how agents communicate, describe their capabilities, or are invoked.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Agents are now first-class actors on the Internet. A single user task can cause an agent to call dozens of APIs and other agents, each of which needs to decide whether to serve the request. Today those services can see a TLS client, an IP address, perhaps an OAuth access token issued to some client, and a User-Agent string that anyone can forge. They cannot reliably tell which agent is calling, who is accountable for it, or whether the protocol metadata it advertises was really published by its operator.

Communication protocols already exist. defines agent-to-agent interaction and an Agent Card; defines how agents reach tools and publishes server metadata; OpenAPI describes HTTP APIs. Each of these describes how to talk to an endpoint. None of them defines a portable answer to who an agent is that works across all of them.
This document defines that missing identity layer:

list.t: A name. The agent URI (e.g., agent://example.com/planner) is a stable, human-readable identifier for an agent ().
A document. Every agent URI maps deterministically to an HTTPS URL that serves an Agent Identity Document listing the agent's operator, public keys, and links to its protocol metadata ().

An anchor. The document is trusted because of where it is served (the origin of the agent URI) or, for agents that need identity to survive a change of domain, because of a Decentralized Identifier ().

Proofs. Agents prove their identity by signing statements about their metadata () and by signing the HTTP requests they make (), including from short-lived instances (). Identity is connected to OAuth 2.0 authorization without new token formats ().
Identify, do not invoke. An agent URI names an agent. It is not a locator for an endpoint and carries no invocation parameters.
Reuse before invent. Every mechanism is a profile of an existing standard: HTTPS and well-known URIs , JWK , JWS , HTTP Message Signatures , OAuth 2.0, and DIDs .
Anchor trust outside the document being verified. A key is trusted because of the origin or DID it is published under, never because a document names it about itself.
Separate the name from the long-lived identity when needed. Domains change hands; agents get renamed and sold. The scheme supports a stable cryptographic identifier behind the human-readable name.
Work for agents that live for seconds. Most agent executions are ephemeral. Instances act under the identity of their agent without being individually published.

section.name: Non-Goals
section.t: The following are explicitly out of scope:

list.t: Communication semantics, message formats, task lifecycles, and invocation. These belong to A2A, MCP, OpenAPI-described APIs, and similar protocols.
Capability, skill, or tool description. Protocol metadata documents (for example, an A2A Agent Card or an MCP server card) remain authoritative for these.
Transport bindings.
Search, ranking, or registry services. This document makes identity verifiable so that any registry can index agents without being trusted.
Reputation, pricing, payments, and service levels.
Authorization policy. Knowing who an agent is does not grant it anything.

section.name: Conventions and Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.
This document uses the terms "JSON object", "member", and "string" from , "origin" from , and "structured field" from .

dd.t: A software system that acts autonomously or semi-autonomously, typically on behalf of a person or organization.
The person or organization accountable for an agent.
An agent URI as defined in . The human-readable name of an agent.
A JSON document, retrieved by dereferencing an agent URI, that describes the agent's operator, keys, and links ().
A public key listed for an agent, used to verify statements, request signatures, and instance credentials made by the agent.
A running, typically short-lived execution of an agent that holds its own key pair and acts under the agent's identity ().
Any party that checks an agent's identity: a website or API receiving requests, an authorization server, a registry, or another agent.

section.name: Overview

figure.title: From agent URI to verifiable identity
figure.artwork: agent://example.com/planner (name) | | deterministic mapping v https://example.com/.well-known/agent/planner (AID URL) | +--------------------+---------------------+ | | | operator keys (JWK Set) links (rel, href) | | origin-anchored: trusted via HTTPS A2A Agent Card, DID-anchored: keys from DID document MCP server card, OAuth client metadata

section.t: A typical verification, for a request received by an API:

list.t: The request carries an HTTP message signature and a Signature-Agent field naming agent://example.com/planner.
The verifier maps the agent URI to its AID URL and retrieves the AID (or uses a cached copy).
The verifier finds the key identified by the signature, checks it is anchored (), and verifies the signature.
The verifier now knows which agent made the request and which operator is accountable. Whether to serve it remains a policy decision.

section.name: Syntax
section.t: The following ABNF uses port and fragment from and ALPHA and DIGIT from .

figure.title: ABNF for the agent URI
figure.sourcecode:
agent-uri = "agent://" agent-host [ name-path ] [ "#" fragment ]
agent-host = dns-name [ ":" port ] dns-name = label *( "." label ) label = let-dig [ *61( let-dig / "-" ) let-dig ] let-dig = ALPHA / DIGIT
name-path = 1*8( "/" name-segment ) name-segment = lc-let-dig [ *61( lc-let-dig / "-" ) lc-let-dig ] lc-let-dig = %x61-7A / DIGIT ; a-z, 0-9

section.t: Additional constraints:

list.t: dns-name MUST be a fully qualified domain name. Internationalized domain names MUST be represented as A-labels . IP literals and userinfo are not permitted.
An agent URI MUST NOT contain a query component.
An agent URI with an empty name-path (e.g., agent://planner.example.com) identifies the domain's root agent.

section.t: Examples:

list.t: agent://example.com/planner#k1 (a reference to key k1 of the agent; see )

section.name: Normalization and Comparison
section.t: The canonical form of an agent URI is produced by:

list.t: Lowercasing the scheme and dns-name.
Converting any U-labels to A-labels.
Removing a port equal to 443.
Removing a single trailing "/" if present.

section.t: Parsers MAY accept input that differs from the ABNF only by the deviations corrected above, and MUST normalize it. Any other deviation (uppercase in name-path, percent-encoding, dot-segments, a query) MUST be rejected.

Two agent URIs identify the same agent if and only if their canonical forms, with any fragment removed, are identical octet strings. In particular, agent://example.com/planner and agent://planner.example.com are different agents, even if the same operator runs both.
Agent URIs in AIDs, statements, signatures, and tokens MUST be in canonical form.

section.name: Dereferencing
section.t: An agent URI is dereferenced by mapping it to the HTTPS URL of its AID:
For example:

texttable.title: Agent URI to AID URL mapping

section.t: The root agent uses the reserved segment _, which cannot appear in a name-segment. This allows the root AID and named AIDs to coexist on static file hosting.
The mapping is purely syntactic. No registry or index needs to be fetched to dereference an agent URI.

section.name: Fragments
section.t: A fragment in an agent URI identifies an Agent Key by its kid (). For example, agent://example.com/planner#k1 refers to the key with "kid": "k1" in the agent's key set. No other fragment semantics are defined.

section.name: Format
section.t: An AID is a JSON object served with media type application/agent-id+json (). It has the following members:

dd.t: REQUIRED. String. The canonical agent URI that this document describes.
REQUIRED. Object identifying who is accountable for the agent, with members name (REQUIRED, string) and url (OPTIONAL, string, HTTPS URL).
REQUIRED for origin-anchored agents; MUST be absent for DID-anchored agents. A JWK Set containing the agent's public keys ().
OPTIONAL. String. A DID whose DID document is the anchor for this agent's keys ().
OPTIONAL. String. A display name for people. It has no identity semantics.
OPTIONAL. String. One of "active" (default), "suspended", or "retired" ().
OPTIONAL. Array of link objects ().
OPTIONAL. String. The time the document was last changed, as an RFC 3339 timestamp.

section.t: Members not defined here MUST be ignored by verifiers that do not understand them. Extension member names SHOULD be namespaced (e.g., "acme_tier") to avoid collision with future versions of this document.
An AID MUST NOT exceed 64 KiB.

section.name: Keys
section.t: Each key in keys MUST:

list.t: contain only public key parameters;
have a kid, which SHOULD be the JWK Thumbprint of the key;
have an alg member; and
be usable for signatures ("use": "sig" or a key_ops containing "verify").

section.t: Implementations MUST support EdDSA (Ed25519) and ES256. Algorithms MUST be restricted as described in ; in particular, none and symmetric algorithms MUST NOT be accepted.

section.name: Links
section.t: Each link object has the following members, with the semantics of Web Linking :

dd.t: REQUIRED. String. A registered link relation type or a URI.
REQUIRED. String. An absolute HTTPS URL.
OPTIONAL. String. The media type of the target.
OPTIONAL. String. An Agent Statement () about the target.

section.t: Link relations expected to be common include:

texttable.title: Common link relations
texttable.c: An OpenAPI or other API description
The agent's OAuth Client ID Metadata Document ()

section.t: A link to a target on the same origin as the agent URI is trusted to the same degree as the AID itself. A link to a target on any other origin MUST carry a statement; verifiers MUST ignore cross-origin links without a valid statement.

section.name: Retrieval and Validation
section.t: To obtain the AID for an agent URI, a verifier:

list.t: Parses and canonicalizes the agent URI (), rejecting it on failure.
Constructs the AID URL ().
Applies the request-destination restrictions of .
Sends an HTTPS GET with Accept: application/agent-id+json, validating the server certificate for dns-name.
Follows redirects only to URLs with the same origin as the AID URL.

Rejects responses larger than 64 KiB, or that are not valid JSON objects. Verifiers MUST NOT reject a response solely because its media type is application/json (to support static hosting) but MUST reject any other media type.
Rejects the document unless its id member is identical to the canonical agent URI.
If did is present, performs the DID binding check of .

section.t: Verifiers SHOULD cache AIDs according to HTTP caching . Operators SHOULD NOT set a freshness lifetime longer than 24 hours, so that key removal takes effect promptly (). Verifiers SHOULD cache failures for a short period to limit repeated fetches.

section.name: Anchoring
section.t: An Agent Key is anchored when the verifier has established that the agent's controller published it. This document defines two anchoring modes. An agent uses exactly one.

section.name: Origin-Anchored Agents
section.t: The AID contains keys and no did. The keys are anchored by the HTTPS retrieval of : control of the agent URI's origin is control of the agent's identity.
This mode needs nothing beyond a web server. Its weakness is that identity is exactly as durable as control of the domain: if the domain lapses or is transferred, so does the agent's identity ().

section.name: DID-Anchored Agents
section.t: The AID contains a did member and no keys. The agent's keys are the verification methods in the DID document's assertionMethod and authentication relationships .
The binding between the agent URI and the DID MUST be bidirectional:

list.t: the AID retrieved for the agent URI names the DID in did; and
the DID document lists the canonical agent URI in its alsoKnownAs property.

section.t: Verifiers MUST check both directions and MUST treat the agent as unverified if either is missing.

DID-anchored agents can change their human-readable name without changing their identity: the operator publishes an AID under the new agent URI and adds the new URI to alsoKnownAs. Verifiers that record the DID (rather than only the agent URI) keep continuity across the rename.

section.name: Lifecycle, Rotation, and Revocation

list.t: Rotation. Operators add the new key, start using it, and remove the old key once signatures made with it are no longer expected to be verified.
Revocation. Removing a key from the AID (or DID document) revokes it. Verifiers learn of revocation when their cached copy expires.

Suspension and retirement. If status is "suspended" or "retired", verifiers MUST treat all signatures and credentials from the agent as invalid. A retired agent URI SHOULD NOT be reassigned to a different agent.

section.t: Operators that need faster or auditable revocation MAY additionally record their AIDs and statements in a transparency service (). This document does not require it.

section.name: Agent Statements
section.t: An Agent Statement is a JWS in compact serialization, signed with an Agent Key, that binds the agent to a specific version of a resource such as an Agent Card. It allows protocol metadata to be served from any origin, mirrored, or included in registries without losing its link to the agent.
The JWS Protected Header MUST contain:

list.t: typ: "agent-statement+jwt";
alg: the algorithm of the signing key;
kid: the agent URI with a fragment identifying the signing key, e.g., "agent://example.com/planner#kPrK_qmxVWaYVA9wwBF6Iuo3vVzz7TxHCTwXBygrS4k".

section.t: The payload is a JWT Claims Set with:

dd.t: REQUIRED. The canonical agent URI.
REQUIRED. The URL of the resource the statement is about.

REQUIRED. An object with members alg ("sha-256"), canon ("jcs" or "none"), and value (the base64url-encoded digest). With "jcs", the digest is computed over the resource canonicalized per ; with "none", over the exact bytes of the representation.
REQUIRED. Issue time.
OPTIONAL. Expiry time. Statements about metadata that changes SHOULD expire.

section.t: To verify a statement, a verifier: checks typ; resolves iss to an AID; checks that the kid agent URI equals iss; locates and checks the anchoring of the key; verifies the signature; checks iat and exp; fetches the resource at sub (or uses a copy); and compares its digest with resource_digest.

Protocol metadata documents that support extension fields SHOULD include a reference back to the agent URI, so that a client starting from the metadata can find the identity. How that reference is expressed is defined by each protocol (see ).

section.name: HTTP Message Signatures Profile
section.t: An agent proves its identity on an HTTP request by signing it with as follows. The profile is designed to be compatible with the architecture of .
The request MUST include a Signature-Agent header field whose value is a structured-field String containing the canonical agent URI:
The signature MUST:

list.t: include the created and expires parameters, with expires no more than 300 seconds after created;
include a keyid parameter whose value is the JWK Thumbprint of the signing key; and
include the parameter tag="agent-uri".

section.t: A nonce parameter SHOULD be included where the verifier is expected to detect replay.
Example:

figure.title: A signed request (line breaks for display only)
figure.sourcecode: POST /v1/bookings HTTP/1.1 Host: api.example.net Content-Type: application/json Content-Digest: sha-256=:...: Signature-Agent: "agent://example.com/planner" Signature-Input: sig1=("@method" "@authority" "@target-uri" "signature-agent" "content-digest");created=1760950000; expires=1760950060; keyid="kPrK_qmxVWaYVA9wwBF6Iuo3vVzz7TxHCTwXBygrS4k"; tag="agent-uri" Signature: sig1=:...:

section.t: A verifier:

list.t: Parses Signature-Agent and canonicalizes the agent URI.
Selects the signature with tag="agent-uri".
Retrieves the AID () and finds an anchored key whose thumbprint equals keyid, or, if an Agent-Instance field is present, validates the instance credential ().
Verifies the signature per and checks that the current time is between created and expires, allowing for modest clock skew.
Checks status ().

section.t: On success, the verifier has established that the request was made by (an instance of) the agent. On failure, the verifier MUST NOT treat the request as coming from the named agent; it MAY process it as an unauthenticated request.

section.name: Agent Instances
section.t: Agents frequently run as many short-lived instances, for example one per task. Publishing a key for each instance in the AID does not scale, and keeping the agent's long-term private key in every instance is unsafe.
Instead, the agent (through its controlling infrastructure) issues each instance an Agent Instance Credential: a JWT signed with an Agent Key, with:

list.t: protected header typ: "agent-instance+jwt" and kid as in ;
iss: the canonical agent URI;
sub: an identifier for the instance, unique per agent and SHOULD be random ();
cnf: a confirmation claim containing the instance's public key as a jwk;
iat and exp. The lifetime SHOULD NOT exceed one hour.

section.t: The instance signs requests with its own key as in , with keyid set to the thumbprint of the instance key, and sends the credential in the Agent-Instance header field as a structured-field String.
The verifier validates the credential against the agent's anchored keys, checks that iss equals the Signature-Agent value, and verifies the request signature using the key in cnf.
This construction is intentionally close to the Workload Identity Token of ; see .

section.name: Authorization
section.t: Identity is not authorization. This section connects agent identity to OAuth 2.0 without defining new token formats.

section.name: The Agent as an OAuth Client
section.t: An agent that obtains OAuth tokens SHOULD use a Client ID Metadata Document as its client identifier and link to it from its AID with rel="oauth-client-metadata". The client metadata document SHOULD include the agent_uri client metadata parameter () containing the canonical agent URI.

An authorization server that sees agent_uri MAY verify it by retrieving the AID and checking that it links to the same client_id. When verified, the authorization server knows which agent the client is and MAY show the agent's identity and operator to the user at consent time.

section.name: Delegation
section.t: When an agent acts on behalf of a user or another agent, the delegation SHOULD be expressed with OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange , with the agent identified in the act claim by "sub" set to its canonical agent URI. As required by , only the current actor is relevant to access-control decisions; nested actors are informational.

Access tokens used by agents SHOULD be sender-constrained, for example with DPoP using the agent's or instance's key, so that a stolen token cannot be used by a different agent. Within a single trust domain, can carry the agent identity and call context between services.

section.name: Protected Resources
section.t: Resource servers advertise their requirements using OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata . A resource server MAY require a valid agent signature () in addition to an access token, and MAY apply policy based on the agent URI, its operator, or its DID.

section.name: Discovery
section.t: Dereferencing a known agent URI requires no discovery. To let others find which agents a domain operates, a domain MAY list them in an API catalog (a linkset ) at /.well-known/api-catalog, using the agent URI as the link context and agent-identity links to the AIDs:

figure.title: Listing agents in an API catalog

section.t: Publishing a catalog is optional (). Registries and search services that index agents SHOULD verify AIDs and statements themselves rather than asking clients to trust the index.

dd.t: An Agent Card describes how to communicate with an agent. The AID links to it with rel="agent-card". A2A clients can verify a card by checking the agent's statement about it.

MCP server metadata describes tools and how to reach them. The AID links to it with rel="mcp-server-card". MCP clients can use the agent URI and request signatures to identify the calling agent to MCP servers.
The AID links to API descriptions with rel="service-desc" .
lets automated clients sign requests and publish keys. This document adds a named, operator-accountable identity and an optional DID anchor on top of the same signature mechanism.

section.name: Trust Model
section.t: For origin-anchored agents, the trust anchors are DNS and the Web PKI: anyone who can obtain a certificate for the agent URI's host and serve content there can impersonate the agent. This is the same trust model as the web itself and is appropriate for most agents. DID-anchored agents can reduce this dependency, at the cost of trusting the DID method's security.

section.name: Handle Reassignment
section.t: If a domain lapses and is registered by someone else, the new holder can publish an AID for the same agent URIs. Verifiers that record identities for audit or reputation SHOULD record the key thumbprint (and DID, when present) alongside the agent URI, and SHOULD treat a change of all keys for an agent as a significant event.

section.name: Request-Destination Restrictions
section.t: Signature-Agent values arrive in requests from untrusted parties, so any verifier can be made to fetch AIDs on attacker-chosen hosts. Verifiers MUST:

list.t: refuse to fetch AID URLs whose host resolves to addresses in the IANA IPv4 and IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registries that are not globally reachable, unless explicitly configured to allow them (e.g., for private deployments);
apply the same check after every redirect and pin the resolved address for the duration of the fetch;
enforce timeouts and the 64 KiB size limit; and
rate-limit fetches per host and cache results, including failures.

section.name: Replay
section.t: Signatures cover the target authority and URI, which prevents replay against a different service. The short created-expires window limits replay against the same service; verifiers for non-idempotent operations SHOULD require and track nonce values.

section.name: Key Compromise
section.t: Compromise of an Agent Key lets the attacker act as the agent until the key is removed and caches expire. Operators SHOULD keep Agent Keys in hardware or a key management service and use instance credentials () so that long-term keys are never present in running agents. Instance credentials SHOULD be short-lived, because they cannot be individually revoked.

section.name: Cross-Origin Metadata
section.t: Requiring statements for cross-origin links () prevents a compromised or malicious third-party host from attaching metadata to an agent's identity. A statement does not vouch for the contents of the resource beyond its integrity: an agent can make false claims in its own Agent Card, and verifiers must not treat identity as an endorsement.

section.name: Confusable Names
section.t: Agent URIs can be visually similar (e.g., examp1e.com). User interfaces that display agent identities SHOULD display the operator name and the A-label form of the domain, and SHOULD warn when a DID-anchored agent's DID is new to the user.

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: The considerations of apply.

list.t: Linkability is the point, for agents. Request signatures make an agent's traffic attributable and linkable across services. That is intended for the agent; it must not extend to the people it acts for. Agent URIs, instance identifiers, and Signature-Agent values MUST NOT encode user identifiers. Instance sub values SHOULD be random and not reused across users.

Per-user agents. Deployments that create one agent per end user (e.g., agent://example.com/u/alice) make that user's activity linkable across all services the agent visits. Such deployments SHOULD use a shared agent identity and convey user context only through authorization tokens sent to parties entitled to it.

Enumeration. API catalogs () let anyone list a domain's agents. Domains that do not want their agents to be enumerable should not publish them in a catalog; AIDs remain retrievable by those who already know the agent URI.
Verifier fetches. Fetching an AID reveals to the operator that a verifier has seen the agent. Caching reduces this signal.

section.t: This document uses the signature tag value agent-uri. Whether a registry entry is needed is an open issue.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

A Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) is a compact sequence of characters that identifies an abstract or physical resource. This specification defines the generic URI syntax and a process for resolving URI references that might be in relative form, along with guidelines and security considerations for the use of URIs on the Internet. The URI syntax defines a grammar that is a superset of all valid URIs, allowing an implementation to parse the common components of a URI reference without knowing the scheme-specific requirements of every possible identifier. This specification does not define a generative grammar for URIs; that task is performed by the individual specifications of each URI scheme. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF

abstract.t: Internet technical specifications often need to define a formal syntax. Over the years, a modified version of Backus-Naur Form (BNF), called Augmented BNF (ABNF), has been popular among many Internet specifications. The current specification documents ABNF. It balances compactness and simplicity with reasonable representational power. The differences between standard BNF and ABNF involve naming rules, repetition, alternatives, order-independence, and value ranges. This specification also supplies additional rule definitions and encoding for a core lexical analyzer of the type common to several Internet specifications. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA): Definitions and Document Framework

abstract.t: This document is one of a collection that, together, describe the protocol and usage context for a revision of Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA), superseding the earlier version. It describes the document collection and provides definitions and other material that are common to the set. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA): Protocol

abstract.t: This document is the revised protocol definition for Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs). The rationale for changes, the relationship to the older specification, and important terminology are provided in other documents. This document specifies the protocol mechanism, called Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA), for registering and looking up IDNs in a way that does not require changes to the DNS itself. IDNA is only meant for processing domain names, not free text. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Media Type Specifications and Registration Procedures

abstract.t: This document defines procedures for the specification and registration of media types for use in HTTP, MIME, and other Internet protocols. This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice.

JSON Web Signature (JWS) represents content secured with digital signatures or Message Authentication Codes (MACs) using JSON-based data structures. Cryptographic algorithms and identifiers for use with this specification are described in the separate JSON Web Algorithms (JWA) specification and an IANA registry defined by that specification. Related encryption capabilities are described in the separate JSON Web Encryption (JWE) specification.

A JSON Web Key (JWK) is a JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) data structure that represents a cryptographic key. This specification also defines a JWK Set JSON data structure that represents a set of JWKs. Cryptographic algorithms and identifiers for use with this specification are described in the separate JSON Web Algorithms (JWA) specification and IANA registries established by that specification.

JSON Web Token (JWT) is a compact, URL-safe means of representing claims to be transferred between two parties. The claims in a JWT are encoded as a JSON object that is used as the payload of a JSON Web Signature (JWS) structure or as the plaintext of a JSON Web Encryption (JWE) structure, enabling the claims to be digitally signed or integrity protected with a Message Authentication Code (MAC) and/or encrypted.

This specification defines mechanisms for dynamically registering OAuth 2.0 clients with authorization servers. Registration requests send a set of desired client metadata values to the authorization server. The resulting registration responses return a client identifier to use at the authorization server and the client metadata values registered for the client. The client can then use this registration information to communicate with the authorization server using the OAuth 2.0 protocol. This specification also defines a set of common client metadata fields and values for clients to use during registration.

front.title: Guidelines and Registration Procedures for URI Schemes

abstract.t: This document updates the guidelines and recommendations, as well as the IANA registration processes, for the definition of Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes. It obsoletes RFC 4395.

This specification defines a method for computing a hash value over a JSON Web Key (JWK). It defines which fields in a JWK are used in the hash computation, the method of creating a canonical form for those fields, and how to convert the resulting Unicode string into a byte sequence to be hashed. The resulting hash value can be used for identifying or selecting the key represented by the JWK that is the subject of the thumbprint.

front.title: The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format

abstract.t: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a lightweight, text-based, language-independent data interchange format. It was derived from the ECMAScript Programming Language Standard. JSON defines a small set of formatting rules for the portable representation of structured data.
This document removes inconsistencies with other specifications of JSON, repairs specification errors, and offers experience-based interoperability guidance.
This specification defines a model for the relationships between resources on the Web ("links") and the type of those relationships ("link relation types").
It also defines the serialisation of such links in HTTP headers with the Link header field.
This memo defines a path prefix for "well-known locations", "/.well-known/", in selected Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.
In doing so, it obsoletes RFC 5785 and updates the URI schemes defined in RFC 7230 to reserve that space. It also updates RFC 7595 to track URI schemes that support well-known URIs in their registry.

front.title: JSON Web Token Best Current Practices

abstract.t: JSON Web Tokens, also known as JWTs, are URL-safe JSON-based security tokens that contain a set of claims that can be signed and/or encrypted. JWTs are being widely used and deployed as a simple security token format in numerous protocols and applications, both in the area of digital identity and in other application areas. This Best Current Practices document updates RFC 7519 to provide actionable guidance leading to secure implementation and deployment of JWTs.

Cryptographic operations like hashing and signing need the data to be expressed in an invariant format so that the operations are reliably repeatable. One way to address this is to create a canonical representation of the data. Canonicalization also permits data to be exchanged in its original form on the "wire" while cryptographic operations performed on the canonicalized counterpart of the data in the producer and consumer endpoints generate consistent results.

This document describes the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS). This specification defines how to create a canonical representation of JSON data by building on the strict serialization methods for JSON primitives defined by ECMAScript, constraining JSON data to the Internet JSON (I-JSON) subset, and by using deterministic property sorting.

The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems. This document describes the overall architecture of HTTP, establishes common terminology, and defines aspects of the protocol that are shared by all versions. In this definition are core protocol elements, extensibility mechanisms, and the "http" and "https" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.
This document updates RFC 3864 and obsoletes RFCs 2818, 7231, 7232, 7233, 7235, 7538, 7615, 7694, and portions of 7230.

The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems. This document defines HTTP caches and the associated header fields that control cache behavior or indicate cacheable response messages.
This document obsoletes RFC 7234.

This document describes a mechanism for creating, encoding, and verifying digital signatures or message authentication codes over components of an HTTP message. This mechanism supports use cases where the full HTTP message may not be known to the signer and where the message may be transformed (e.g., by intermediaries) before reaching the verifier. This document also describes a means for requesting that a signature be applied to a subsequent HTTP message in an ongoing HTTP exchange.

This document defines HTTP fields that support integrity digests. The Content-Digest field can be used for the integrity of HTTP message content. The Repr-Digest field can be used for the integrity of HTTP representations. Want-Content-Digest and Want-Repr-Digest can be used to indicate a sender's interest and preferences for receiving the respective Integrity fields.
This document obsoletes RFC 3230 and the Digest and Want-Digest HTTP fields.

This document describes a set of data types and associated algorithms that are intended to make it easier and safer to define and handle HTTP header and trailer fields, known as "Structured Fields", "Structured Headers", or "Structured Trailers". It is intended for use by specifications of new HTTP fields.
This document obsoletes RFC 8941.

This document offers guidance for developing privacy considerations for inclusion in protocol specifications. It aims to make designers, implementers, and users of Internet protocols aware of privacy-related design choices. It suggests that whether any individual RFC warrants a specific privacy considerations section will depend on the document's content.

This specification defines a protocol for an HTTP- and JSON-based Security Token Service (STS) by defining how to request and obtain security tokens from OAuth 2.0 authorization servers, including security tokens employing impersonation and delegation.

front.title: Linkset: Media Types and a Link Relation Type for Link Sets

abstract.t: This specification defines two formats and associated media types for representing sets of links as standalone documents. One format is based on JSON, and the other is aligned with the format for representing links in the HTTP "Link" header field. This specification also introduces a link relation type to support the discovery of sets of links.

This document describes a mechanism for sender-constraining OAuth 2.0 tokens via a proof-of-possession mechanism on the application level. This mechanism allows for the detection of replay attacks with access and refresh tokens.

front.title: api-catalog: A Well-Known URI and Link Relation to Help Discovery of APIs

abstract.t: This document defines the "api-catalog" well-known URI and link relation. It is intended to facilitate automated discovery and usage of published Application Programming Interfaces (APIs). A request to the api-catalog resource will return a document providing information about, and links to, the Publisher's APIs.
This specification defines a metadata format that an OAuth 2.0 client or authorization server can use to obtain the information needed to interact with an OAuth 2.0 protected resource.

section.name: Open Issues
section.t: This appendix will be removed before publication.

list.t: Web Bot Auth alignment. uses Signature-Agent to point at a key directory URL. Decide whether agent URIs become a permitted value of that field, whether the AID also serves as (or links to) an HTTP message signatures directory, or whether a distinct field is needed.
WIMSE alignment. Decide whether Agent Instance Credentials should be a profile of the WIMSE Workload Identity Token with iss set to the agent URI, rather than a separate type.

Back-references from protocol metadata. Agree with the A2A and MCP projects on how an Agent Card or MCP server card names its agent URI, and who registers the agent-card and mcp-server-card link relations.
Reserved root segment. /.well-known/agent/_ is chosen to work on static hosting. Alternatives (a separate well-known suffix for the root agent) should be evaluated.
Name path depth and character set. Lowercase LDH segments, at most 8, are chosen for unambiguous comparison. Confirm this is sufficient for multi-tenant platforms.
DNS-based verification. Consider an alternative proof of control via a DNS TXT record (as for some handle systems), for operators that cannot serve well-known paths.
Revocation latency. Evaluate whether cache lifetimes alone are adequate, or whether a status list or transparency log should be RECOMMENDED.
Port. Confirm that non-default ports should be permitted in agent identities at all, given they complicate certificate and policy handling.

section.name: Changes from draft-narvaneni-agent-uri-03
section.t: This revision changes the scope of the document from "addressing and discovery" to "identity".
Removed:

list.t: agent+<protocol> transport-binding schemes and the Transport Bindings registry.
Invocation semantics (GET/POST rules, fallback behaviour), query parameters in agent URIs, and conformance levels.
The /.well-known/agents.json registry, replaced by the deterministic mapping of and optional RFC 9727 catalogs.
The agent descriptor's capability fields (skills, transport, interactionModel, versioning, content negotiation). Protocol metadata documents are linked instead.
DID authorities in agent URIs, replaced by DID anchoring ().
Cross-cutting conventions (tracing, idempotency, rate limits, health) and the Interaction Models registry.
The monotonic scope narrowing rule, which conflicted with .

section.t: Added:

list.t: Strict URI syntax, normalization, and comparison rules.
The Agent Identity Document and anchoring modes.
Agent Statements, the HTTP Message Signatures profile, and Agent Instance Credentials.
OAuth client and delegation bindings.
Security and privacy considerations specific to agent identity.
